doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Miles Davis quintet and tunes as launching pads
summary: Weiss explains that Miles's group played the same tunes nightly because they were launching pads, and that the Cookers use a few staple tunes the same way.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: and Tony, why did they play “Autumn Leaves” every night when they were recording “ESP?” You know? Why was their set, I mean as far as the material they chose, basically the same every night for three — and over the three years they added a few things, but for the most part they were playing “Footprints” I mean they added some new tunes. They added “Footprints” and they added “Agitation” but they still played “’Round Midnight” and they had a set. And it was like why do you think those guys played those tunes all the time? And it was ‘cause they knew that they could do anything on them. They were launching pads for them to do their thing you know. And you could listen to five Miles Davis’ concerts in a row and those tunes are different every time. You know? What Herbie, Ron, and Tony did was never pat. It was challenging every night and they challenged each other every night and they did everything. I mean they’re the penultimate rhythm section but that point is clear. I mean you know, you make new records for new material for fans. But you find the stuff to do live that is the launching point for you to continue to do what you do, or that gives you the openness to try that thing and you know the thing so if you miss you can get back on track. And we’ve continue that. I mean we do new records all the time and some of those tunes always make their way into the book. Some make their way into the book for a while and go away when something else comes along, but there’s still three or four staples that we basically have done almost from the beginning, until something comes along that displaces it. And it’s not like oh we’re playing that tune again. It’s like okay well what are we going to do with that tune tonight? You know? What’s going to happen? You know. And there’s no talk of let’s do something innovative on that tune tonight. It’s whatever grows out of our experience of playing together and doing this stuff and everybody knowing each other well enough to be like go ahead. So things can happen. And I’ve always tried to have bands that do that. And you know you miss more, you know you take more chances, but when it works I mean Miles missed. He missed bad. But it was the same with Herbie, Ron, and Tony, I can hear, now that I know the material I can hear when they missed things, but they’re just so much better at it you can’t really detect it. But I mean it’s really all — I mean what I’ve found is it’s really all about approach. I mean yeah, we’re going to sit down and write a lot of great music, but how it’s played on the bandstand it’s really all about approach and the person’s approach to the music. I mean I stick with those guys because they’re great, but they also teach me that every night. And I’m the one who’s maybe more locked into a certain thing by what I play but they’ll push me towards that. Like you know I don’t want to — say I play a certain tune and I like a certain phrases over it or something. I only seemingly play it when everything is not connect — it’s like a fallback. Or it’s something that gets started and then let’s see where you take me today.
